author: wonder-full
final_message:
All five versions are implemented and pass every sample byte-for-byte.

**Algorithm (same in all five).**
Read the whole file into memory as bytes.
Split on `\n` and validate each line with a hand-written scanner that implements the SPEC regex exactly (fixed-position timestamp checks, `[a-z]+-\d+` server, exact method token, path charset, optional `?` query up to the next space, 3-digit status, `\d+B`, `\d+\.\d ms`, and a closing `"` as the last character).
No regex engine is used anywhere.
For well-formed lines, count the status class in a 10-slot array, build the path template in a reused scratch buffer (all-digit segments become `{id}`), and append the latency (as integer tenths, 64-bit) to that template's list.
At the end, sort templates by count descending then template ascending, sort only the top 10 latency lists, and take p50/p95 by the nearest-rank rule `(p*n+99)/100`.
Latencies print as `v/10` `.` `v%10`.

**Main speed choices per language.**

- [cpp/main.cpp](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/cpp/main.cpp): `fread` of the whole file, `memchr` line splitting, custom open-addressing hash table (FNV-1a computed while building the template in a raw scratch buffer, so strings allocate only on first sight of a template), `vector<int64_t>` latencies, stdout set to binary mode so output is LF-only like the samples.
- [java/src/Main.java](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/java/src/Main.java): `Files.readAllBytes`, parsing on the raw `byte[]` with no per-line allocation, same custom open-addressing table keyed by `byte[]` templates, primitive `long[]` latency lists with manual growth, one `StringBuilder` for output.
- [csharp/Program.cs](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/csharp/Program.cs): `File.ReadAllBytes` plus `unsafe` pointer parsing over a pinned array, `ReadOnlySpan.IndexOf` for newline search, custom open-addressing table over scratch bytes, `long[]` latency lists, one `StringBuilder` write. The [solution.csproj](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/csharp/solution.csproj) is unchanged.
- [go/main.go](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/go/main.go): `os.ReadFile`, `bytes.IndexByte` line splitting, template built into a reused `[]byte` and looked up with `map[string]*entry` using the allocation-free `m[string(b)]` lookup idiom (a copy is made only on insert), `[]int64` latencies, output built with `strconv.AppendInt` into one buffer.
- [js/main.js](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions-langs/wonder-full/logscan/js/main.js): `fs.readFileSync` into a `Buffer`, native `Buffer.indexOf(10, …)` line splitting, byte-wise parsing on the `Uint8Array`, custom open-addressing table (`Int32Array`) over template bytes with a 32-bit FNV hash via `Math.imul`, strings decoded only for newly seen templates, numeric array sort for the top 10.

**Test results.**
All five versions produce byte-identical output to `s1.out`, `s2.out` and `s3.out` for the corresponding inputs.
Beyond the samples, I differential-tested all five against an independent Python implementation using the SPEC regex with `re.fullmatch`: ~3,100 generated edge/fuzz lines (all methods and near-misses, empty/minimal lines, `/` and `/?` paths, digit-segment variants, tab-in-query, bad timestamps/servers/sizes/latencies, unterminated or over-long user agents, status classes 0xx–9xx, a 10-digit latency, percentile sets, tie-breaking), plus an empty file and a single-empty-line file. All five matched the reference on every case.

Indicative speed on a synthetic 2,000,000-line / 228 MB input (best of 3, machine also busy): C++ 0.67 s, Go 0.73 s, C# 0.87 s, Java 1.28 s, JS 1.32 s.

One local note: `cpp\build.cmd` initially failed in my shell because the inherited `PATH` was over 8,000 characters, which overflowed `vcvars64.bat`. With a trimmed `PATH` it builds cleanly. No build scripts were changed.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
